tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: This tour begins at the root README.md, which introduces the openapi-generator service — a Go-backed tool that generates OpenAPI specs from frisboo-core-banking APIs, with a React/TypeScript frontend. The Makefile serves as the single build entry point orchestrating both the Go backend and the TypeScript frontend, while go.mod declares the module path (frisboo-bank/openapi-generator-service) and its direct dependencies. Together these three files establish the project's scope, build workflow, and module identity before diving into code.

tour.title: CLI Entry Point & Bootstrap
tour.description: The journey enters the codebase through api/cmd/main.go — the single CLI entry point that bootstraps the entire application. From there, the application.go contract defines the Application interface, while application_builder.go orchestrates the dependency wiring by composing modules (HTTP, mediator, container, config, etc.) into a runnable application. The bootstrap.go file ties it all together, invoking the builder to construct and start the service. This step reveals the application's top-level architecture: a cobra-driven CLI that assembles a modular, dependency-injected runtime.
tour.languageLesson: Go application bootstrap pattern: a central main.go calls an ApplicationBuilder that composes modules via a DI container. Each module registers its providers (constructors, interfaces, configurations) into the container, which then resolves the full dependency graph at startup. This keeps wiring logic separate from business logic.

tour.title: Configuration & DI Foundation
tour.description: Before any service can run, configuration must be loaded. The config_loader.go file provides a Viper-backed, thread-safe lazy loader with mapstructure hooks for decoding environment-specific settings. The config_module.go registers the configuration system into the DI container, while environment_module.go handles environment-specific enum resolution. This step establishes how the application reads settings (database URLs, log levels, cache configs) and makes them available throughout the dependency graph.

tour.title: HTTP / API Layer
tour.description: With configuration and bootstrap in place, the HTTP server comes into focus. The echo_adapter.go implements the HTTPServer interface using the Echo framework, handling server lifecycle, middleware, and route listing. The http_server.go contract defines the abstraction, while route_builder.go and route_group.go construct the routing tree that maps URL patterns to handlers. The chrome_devtools_endpoint.go demonstrates a concrete endpoint, and the apis_module.go wires the entire HTTP layer into the application. This step shows how external requests flow into the system.
tour.languageLesson: Adapter pattern in Go: the Echo framework is hidden behind an HTTPServer interface. This allows swapping the underlying HTTP framework (e.g., from Echo to net/http or Gin) without changing route definitions, middleware, or endpoint handlers — the adapter translates between framework-specific types and the project's abstractions.

tour.title: Service & Business Logic
tour.description: Now that requests arrive via HTTP, the service layer processes them. The entities_module.go defines the entity domain module, while the mediator.go implements the CQRS mediator pattern that dispatches queries and commands to their handlers. The list_entities_handler.go processes a list-entities query, transforming the request through entity_dto.go (data transfer objects) and entity_mapper.go (domain mapping). This step reveals how business use cases are organized: queries flow through the mediator to handlers, which orchestrate domain logic and return DTOs back to the API layer.
tour.languageLesson: CQRS + Mediator pattern: queries (e.g., ListEntities) are separate objects dispatched through a mediator to dedicated handlers. This decouples callers from handlers, enables cross-cutting concerns (validation, logging, caching) as mediator pipeline behaviors, and makes the request flow explicit and testable.

tour.title: Data Persistence Layer
tour.description: Business logic needs data, which comes from the persistence layer. The entity_repository_pgx.go implements the entity repository using pgx — the high-performance PostgreSQL driver — and is the most connected node in the graph (41 outgoing edges, 45 weighted fan-out). The entity_model.go maps domain entities to database columns, while the postgresx_adapter.go provides the pgx-specific connection and transaction implementation behind the sql_client.go contract. This step shows how the abstract repository interface is backed by a concrete PostgreSQL implementation, with the SQL client abstraction isolating driver-specific code.
tour.languageLesson: Repository pattern with pgx: the domain code depends on an entity_repository interface, not a concrete implementation. The pgx repository translates domain queries into SQL using the sql_client abstraction, which itself is interface-driven — allowing swaps between pg (standard lib) and pgx (high-performance) drivers without touching domain code.

tour.title: Database Migrations
tour.description: The schema that the persistence layer targets is defined through SQL migrations. The 000003_create_entities_table.sql creates the core entities table (with the entities table node visible in the graph), while earlier migrations enable extensions and create system tables. The goose_adapter.go wraps the goose migration runner, and the migration_module.go integrates migrations into the DI container so they run automatically on startup. This step connects the Go code to its persistent storage, showing how schema evolution is managed versioned, reversible, and integrated with the application lifecycle.
tour.languageLesson: Goose migration pattern: SQL files are numbered sequentially (000001, 000002, …) and applied by goose, which tracks version in a schema_migrations table. The goose_adapter wraps this into the DI system, so migrations run as part of application startup — a simple, language-agnostic approach to schema evolution that keeps SQL and Go in sync.

tour.title: Cross-Cutting: Logger, Cache & RPC
tour.description: With the core request path established, this step explores the cross-cutting concerns that run alongside every operation. The zerolog_adapter.go implements the logger contract using zerolog (a fast, structured JSON logger), registered via logger_module.go. The redis_adapter.go provides a Redis-backed cache implementation behind the cache.go contract, with memory_adapter.go as a fallback. The grpc_adapter.go exposes a gRPC server for internal service-to-service communication, wired through rpc_server_module.go. These three subsystems — observability, performance, and inter-service RPC — are modular and swappable via their interfaces.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-adapter pattern: logging, caching, and RPC each define a contract (interface) with multiple concrete adapters (zerolog for logger, redis/memory for cache, gRPC for RPC). The DI container selects the active adapter via configuration, making cross-cutting concerns interchangeable without changing business code — a cornerstone of clean Go architecture.

tour.title: Query & Pagination
tour.description: Listing entities requires more than a simple SQL query — it needs filtering, sorting, and pagination. The list_query.go defines a generic list query object, while query_filters.go and query_orders.go build filter and order expressions using a composable builder pattern. The filter_comparison.go, logical_operator.go, and search_condition.go enums provide the vocabulary for expressing complex WHERE clauses. This step shows how the query layer abstracts database-specific concerns into a reusable, type-safe query model that handlers and repositories consume.
tour.languageLesson: Composable query builder: filter conditions (comparison, IN, BETWEEN, search) and logical operators (AND, OR) are combined into a tree structure that the SQL repository translates into parameterized queries. The enum-driven design ensures only valid filter types are constructed, and the builder pattern keeps query assembly readable and testable.

tour.title: Frontend UI Layer
tour.description: The backend's gRPC API is consumed by a React/TypeScript frontend. The index.tsx is the React entry point, App.tsx is the root component, and EntitiesList.tsx renders the entity list using TanStack Query for data fetching. The generated protobuf/gRPC client bindings — entity_service_pb.js and entity_service-EntityService_connectquery.js — provide typed API clients auto-generated from buf/protobuf definitions. This step completes the full-stack picture: Go backend → protobuf → generated TypeScript client → React UI, showing how the spec-driven architecture flows end-to-end.
tour.languageLesson: Protobuf field-number permanence: the generated client code is tied to protobuf field numbers, not field names. Renaming a protobuf field is safe, but changing its number breaks wire compatibility. This is why buf.yaml and buf.gen.yaml govern code generation — they ensure the Go server and TypeScript client always share the same schema contract.

tour.title: Infrastructure & Build Tooling
tour.description: The tour moves from application code to the infrastructure that supports it. The docker-compose.yaml defines three local services — PostgreSQL 18, Redis 8, and NATS 2 with JetStream — on a shared network with healthchecks and persistent volumes. The Makefile orchestrates build, test, lint, and run targets for both Go and TypeScript sub-projects. The buf.yaml and buf.gen.yaml configure protobuf code generation, while .golangci.yml, revive-config.toml, and rslint.config.ts govern linting across languages. The .air.toml enables live-reloading for Go development. This step shows the DevOps scaffolding that makes development and CI/CD repeatable.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Makefile targets: the Makefile uses phony targets (build, test, lint, run) as a unified interface across Go and TypeScript. Each target delegates to the appropriate sub-project toolchain (go build, pnpm test, golangci-lint, rstest), allowing developers to run `make test` without knowing which language a given artifact is written in.

tour.title: Configuration & Validation
tour.description: The final step ties together the declarative configuration and validation systems. The application.yaml holds environment-specific settings (database, logging, cache, RPC endpoints), while application.development.yaml-l provides layered overrides. The validator.go and validatable.go implement a validation framework that enforces business rules on DTOs before they reach the handler. On the frontend side, tsconfig.json and package.json define the TypeScript build and dependency graph. This step closes the loop: configuration flows from YAML → Viper → DI container → services, while validation guards the boundary between HTTP input and domain logic.
tour.languageLesson: Interface-driven validation: DTOs implement a Validatable interface that the mediator pipeline invokes before dispatching to handlers. This keeps validation logic co-located with the types it validates, and the validator.go provides reusable assertion helpers — a common Go pattern for declarative, testable input validation.
